abide.gloss: To put up with something; in older usage, to stay or dwell somewhere.

senses.head: Tolerate, put up with
senses.body: Almost always negative — *cannot abide*, *could not abide*. This is the only sense alive in everyday American English, and it takes the regular *abided*.
examples: I cannot *abide* people who talk during a movie.
She could not *abide* the noise from the construction site.
He has never *abided* criticism well.

senses.head: Abide by — comply with
senses.body: Fixed phrasal use, and always regular: *abided by*, never the strong form.
examples: We *abided by* the ruling even though we disagreed.
Everyone here *abides by* the same rules.
The company *has abided by* every term of the settlement.

senses.head: Dwell, remain
senses.body: Archaic and literary. This is the sense that takes *abode*, which survives far more healthily as a noun — *a humble abode*.
examples: Her family *abode* in that valley for four generations.
The shepherds *have abode* in these hills since before the road was built.
A strange quiet *abides* in that house.

alight.gloss: To come down and settle on something, or to step down out of a vehicle.

senses.head: Land, settle on something
senses.body: The core sense, used of birds, insects, and anything that comes lightly to rest. Both *alit* and the regular *alighted* are standard.
examples: Sparrows *alight* on the feeder the moment I go back inside.
A cardinal *alit* on the railing and stared at us.
The same dragonfly *has alit* on that reed all afternoon.

senses.head: Step down from a vehicle
senses.body: Formal, and commonest in transit announcements and British signage; ordinary American speech says *get off*.
examples: She *alights* at the Franklin Street stop every morning.
Two passengers *had alit* before the conductor noticed the open door.

senses.head: Alight on — happen upon
senses.body: Literary, used of a gaze or a thought coming to rest on something. Usually regular here: *alighted on*.
examples: Her eye *alighted on* the one sentence that mattered.
We *have alit on* a compromise that might actually work.

baby-sit.gloss: To look after someone else's children while the parents are out.

senses.head: Look after children
senses.body: The everyday sense. Modern American style writes the word solid — *babysit, babysat* — and the hyphen now looks dated.
examples: I *baby-sit* for the Novaks most Friday nights.
She *baby-sat* my nephews all through high school.
We *have baby-sat* for them twice this month already.
My brother *baby-sits* whenever he needs gas money.

senses.head: Keep an idle watch over something
senses.body: Informal and slightly resentful: to sit with a process or a person that ought not need supervising.
examples: Somebody has to *baby-sit* the build until it finishes.
He *baby-sat* the server all night waiting for the migration to clear.
I *have baby-sat* that spreadsheet for three days.

senses.head: Light from behind
senses.body: Photography and stage lighting. Like *light*, it also allows a regular *backlighted*, but *backlit* is far commoner.
examples: We *backlight* the product shots to lift them off the wall.
The photographer *backlit* her subject with a single strobe.
They *have backlit* every sign in the terminal.
He *backlights* the stage with two amber panels.

senses.head: Backlit — lit from behind
senses.body: Almost always passive or in front of a noun: *a backlit screen*, *a backlit keyboard*.
examples: The keyboard *had* been *backlit* in blue since the last update.
Every display in the lobby *is backlit* around the clock.

backslide.gloss: To slip back into a bad habit, an abandoned belief, or an earlier and worse condition.

senses.head: Relapse into an old habit
senses.body: The everyday sense, used of diets, sobriety, and any effort at self-improvement.
examples: Dieters *backslide* around the holidays.
He *backslid* the week after he quit smoking.
She *has backslid* twice since January.

senses.head: Fall away from faith
senses.body: Religious register, and the original sense. In that writing you will also meet the participle *backslidden*.
examples: The preacher warned that a believer can *backslide* without ever noticing it.
Two of the congregation *had backslid* by the following spring.

senses.head: Regress, lose ground
senses.body: Of institutions, countries, or measured results. Common in journalism: *democratic backsliding*.
examples: The department *backslides* every time the budget tightens.
Several districts *have backslid* on reading scores.
By March the government *had backslid* on every reform it promised.

beget.gloss: To father a child; more broadly, to cause something to come into being.

senses.head: Give rise to, cause
senses.body: The living use, and it lives mostly in aphorisms and headlines. Formal; ordinary speech says *leads to*.
examples: Violence *begets* violence.
Cheap money can *beget* speculation.
That one decision *has begot* a decade of lawsuits.
The scandal *had begot* three investigations before anyone resigned.

senses.head: Father a child
senses.body: Biblical and formal, and only ever of the father. The archaic participle *begotten* is the form most Americans recognize — *his only begotten son*.
examples: Abraham *begot* Isaac.
He *had begotten* seven children by the time he was forty.

behold.gloss: To look at something, especially something striking.

senses.head: Look upon, gaze at
senses.body: Literary or ceremonial; nobody says it in ordinary conversation. Do not confuse it with the adjective *beholden*, meaning indebted, which is a different word.
examples: The crowd *beheld* the eclipse in complete silence.
Few travelers *have beheld* that valley under snow.
She *beholds* the city each morning from the same window.

senses.head: Behold! — presenting something
senses.body: Imperative only, and today usually playful or ironic when a thing is revealed.
examples: *Behold* the size of that canyon.
He opened the box and — *behold* — the missing part was inside.

senses.head: Lo and behold
senses.body: A frozen phrase introducing a surprise. It is the only place most Americans ever use the verb.
examples: We drove all that way and, lo and *behold*, the museum was closed.
I looked again and, lo and *behold*, the keys were sitting on the counter.
Nobody who *had beheld* the wreck could describe it calmly.

betide.gloss: To happen to someone, especially to happen badly.

senses.head: Woe betide — a warning
senses.body: The one frozen phrase that keeps this verb alive. It is a subjunctive, so it normally takes no ending, though *woe betides* also turns up.
examples: Woe *betide* the student who forgets that deadline.
Woe *betide* anyone who touches my coffee.
Woe *betides* the traveler who ignores that sign.

senses.head: Happen, befall
senses.body: Archaic outside of the phrase above; the past *betid* is museum English.
examples: Whatever may *betide*, we will meet again in spring.
Great sorrow *betid* the household that winter.
Stranger things *had betid* the village before the bridge was built.

bide.gloss: To wait, especially to wait for the right moment.

senses.head: Bide one's time
senses.body: The one living use, and there Americans say *bided*. Do not confuse it with the separate regular verb *bode*, to be a sign of something — *this bodes well*.
examples: *Bide* your time and the price will come down.
She *bides* her time better than anyone I know.
He *bided* his time until the market turned.
They *have bided* their time long enough.

senses.head: Stay, dwell, remain
senses.body: Archaic and dialectal, and the sense that carries the strong forms *bode*, *bode*.
examples: The old sailor *bode* his time ashore for a year.
He *had bode* in that harbor town all winter, waiting for a berth.

bind.gloss: To tie things together, to place someone under an obligation, or to make separate things hold fast to each other.

senses.head: Tie, fasten together
senses.body: The literal core sense: joining things with rope, twine, wire, or tape.
examples: We *bind* the reports in black covers.
She *bound* the stack of letters with kitchen twine.
Someone *has bound* all the cables with zip ties.

senses.head: Place under an obligation
senses.body: Legal and contractual, and the reason *binding* is an adjective in its own right.
examples: The contract *binds* both parties for five years.
He *has bound* himself to a two-year lease.
The treaty *had bound* them long before the war started.

senses.head: Be bound to; be bound for
senses.body: Two frozen adjectival uses of the participle: *bound to* means certain to, and *bound for* means headed for. Neither behaves like an ordinary passive.
examples: Something like this *was bound to* happen eventually.
We were on a train *bound for* Chicago.

senses.head: Hold together, unite
senses.body: Figurative, of what holds a group or a story together.
examples: Shared work *binds* a crew faster than anything else.
Grief *had bound* the two families together for good.

senses.head: Bind a book
senses.body: The bookbinding sense; the trade is called *binding*.
examples: That shop still *binds* dissertations by hand.
They *bound* my grandfather's letters into a single volume.

senses.head: Bind a wound; bind up
senses.body: Somewhat formal or biblical; everyday speech says *bandage*.
examples: Medics *bind* the wound before they move anyone.
She *bound up* his arm with a torn shirt.

senses.head: Hold fast; stick, jam
senses.body: Intransitive, used of a mixture that comes together and of a mechanism that seizes.
examples: An egg helps the mixture *bind*.
The drawer *binds* whenever the wood swells.
The brake *has bound* against the rotor since the last repair.

senses.head: Bind to (chemistry, computing)
senses.body: Technical, but a learner meets it constantly in science writing and in software documentation.
examples: The antibody *binds* to a protein on the cell surface.
The molecule *has bound* to the receptor site.
We *bound* the shortcut to a different key.

bleed.gloss: To lose blood, or to let a fluid drain slowly out of something.

senses.head: Lose blood
senses.body: The literal sense. Never the regular form — the past is always *bled*.
examples: Cuts on the scalp *bleed* more than they should.
His nose *bled* for ten minutes.
She *had bled* through two bandages before the nurse came back.

senses.head: Bleed a line, drain fluid
senses.body: Transitive and technical: *bleed the brakes*, *bleed a radiator*. It keeps the strong form too.
examples: You have to *bleed* the brakes after changing the lines.
He *bled* the radiator to stop the knocking.
The mechanic *has bled* every line on the car.

senses.head: Lose money steadily
senses.body: Business writing, either intransitive or with cash as the object.
examples: The company *bleeds* cash every quarter.
The fund *bled* investors for three straight years.

senses.head: Run, spread (of color or ink)
senses.body: Of dye in the wash and of ink on paper.
examples: Cheap dye *bleeds* in hot water.
The red *had bled* into the collar before she noticed.

senses.head: Bleed into — blur together
senses.body: Figurative, of boundaries that fail to hold.
examples: Work *bleeds* into the weekend if you let it.
The two chapters *have bled* into each other.

senses.head: One's heart bleeds
senses.ru: сердце обливается кровью, всей душой сочувствовать
senses.body: A fixed sympathy phrase, and in American speech usually sarcastic.
examples: My heart *bleeds* for anyone driving in this.
We *bled* for that family when the story came out.

breastfeed.gloss: To feed a baby with milk from the breast.

senses.head: Nurse a baby
senses.body: Used with or without an object: you can *breastfeed a baby* or simply *breastfeed*.
examples: Many mothers *breastfeed* for the first six months.
She *breastfed* both of her children.
They *have breastfed* longer than the pediatrician expected.
My sister *breastfeeds* in public without a second thought.

senses.head: Breastfed — raised on breast milk
senses.body: The participle used as an adjective, common in medical and parenting writing.
examples: *Breastfed* infants show a different gut flora.
By the time the twins were weaned she *had breastfed* for two solid years.

breed.gloss: To produce offspring, to raise animals or plants for chosen traits, or to give rise to something.

senses.head: Raise selectively, develop a strain
senses.body: Transitive, of animals and plants bred toward a purpose.
examples: They *bred* quarter horses on that farm for sixty years.
The kennel *breeds* only two litters a year.
Those roses *had* been *bred* for cold winters.

senses.head: Reproduce, have young
senses.body: Intransitive, and used of animals rather than people.
examples: Rabbits *breed* fast.
The herons *have bred* on that island for decades.

senses.head: Give rise to, produce
senses.body: Figurative, of conditions producing feelings or behavior. The proverb is *familiarity breeds contempt*.
examples: Familiarity *has bred* a certain carelessness around here.
Delay *breeds* rumor.
The shortage *bred* a black market almost overnight.

senses.head: Bring up, raise (a person)
senses.body: Now almost only in fixed phrases: *born and bred*, *bred in the bone*, *well-bred*. The past *bred* is a homophone of *bread*, which is where the misspelling comes from.
examples: He was born and *bred* in Tulsa.
That caution *had* been *bred* into her since childhood.

senses.head: Scold, reproach gently
senses.body: Formal and a little literary. Modern American English makes it regular — *chided, chided* — and the strong *chid* and *chidden* now read as archaic.
examples: She *chides* me whenever I skip breakfast.
Do not *chide* him for a mistake he did not make.
The teacher *chid* the class for its sloppy handwriting.
He *has chid* his brother about that car a hundred times.

senses.head: Chide someone into silence
senses.body: The verb takes a direction: scolding used to move someone toward or away from an action.
examples: Their mother *had chid* them into silence before the guests arrived.
She *chided* him out of buying the thing at all.

climb.gloss: To go up something using hands and feet, or simply to rise.

senses.head: Go up using hands and feet
senses.body: The core sense. Standard American English is regular here — *climb, climbed, climbed*; *clumb* is a dialect past you meet in Twain and in older Southern and Appalachian speech, never in edited prose.
examples: We *climb* that ridge every Fourth of July.
She *climbs* like she was born on a rock wall.
He *clumb* that fence quicker than a cat.
They *had clumb* halfway up the water tower before anybody hollered.

senses.head: Rise, increase
senses.body: Of any measured quantity going up steadily.
examples: Prices *climb* every summer.
The temperature *has climbed* six degrees since noon.

senses.head: Climb into, climb out of
senses.body: Always with a preposition: *climb into bed*, *climb out of a truck*, *climb through a window*.
examples: He *climbed* into the truck without a word.
She *has climbed* in and out of that attic all morning.

senses.head: Rise in rank or standing
senses.body: Figurative, and usually with a ladder or a chart in the picture.
examples: She *climbed* from clerk to partner in nine years.
The song *has climbed* to number three.

senses.head: Slope or grow upward
senses.body: Of plants that grow up a support and of roads that rise.
examples: Ivy *climbs* the whole north wall.
The road *climbs* for six miles after the bridge.

senses.head: Gain altitude (of an aircraft)
senses.body: Aviation, intransitive.
examples: The plane *climbs* to cruising altitude in about twelve minutes.
We *had climbed* to thirty thousand feet before the seatbelt sign went off.

cling.gloss: To hold on tightly, or to stick to a surface.

senses.head: Hold on tightly
senses.body: Physical grip, usually out of fear or need. There is no form *clinged*.
examples: The toddler *clung* to her father's leg.
She *had clung* to the railing until the ferry steadied.
Climbers *cling* to that wall with their fingertips.

senses.head: Stick to a surface
senses.body: Of wet, static, or smelly things that will not come off.
examples: Wet leaves *cling* to the windshield.
Static *clings* to everything in this dry air.
The campfire smell *has clung* to that coat for a week.

senses.head: Cling to a belief
senses.body: Figurative, and it usually implies the thing is not worth holding.
examples: He *has clung* to that theory for thirty years.
They *clung* to the hope that the flight would be rerouted.

senses.head: Cling to a person
senses.ru: льнуть, не отходить ни на шаг
senses.body: Emotional dependence, and the source of the adjective *clingy*.
examples: He *clings* to whoever pays him attention.
The puppy *clung* to us for a solid week.

crossbreed.gloss: To breed two different varieties or species together.

senses.head: Breed two varieties together
senses.body: Transitive, and deliberate — the work of a breeder or a lab.
examples: Growers *crossbreed* these apples for firmness.
The lab *crossbred* the two strains last spring.
Ranchers *have crossbred* Angus and Hereford cattle for generations.

senses.head: Breed across a line naturally
senses.body: Intransitive, with no breeder involved.
examples: The two populations *crossbreed* wherever their ranges overlap.
Domestic cats and wildcats *have crossbred* in that valley for centuries.

senses.head: Blend two unlike things
senses.body: Figurative, of genres, designs, or ideas spliced together.
examples: The show *crossbreeds* a courtroom drama with a sitcom.
Someone *had crossbred* a pickup and a sports car and called it innovation.

dig.gloss: To break up and move earth, or to make a hole in something.

senses.head: Excavate, make a hole
senses.body: The literal core sense, of people, animals, and machines.
examples: They *dig* a new well every few years.
The dog *dug* under the fence again.
Crews *have dug* three feet down and hit rock.

senses.head: Dig up, dig out — unearth
senses.body: Literal for potatoes and fossils, figurative for old records and old grudges.
examples: She *dug out* the old lease from a box in the garage.
Reporters *have dug up* three more emails.

senses.head: Dig into — investigate
senses.body: Figurative, of research and scrutiny.
examples: He *digs* through the archive whenever he needs a story.
The committee *has dug into* the contracts line by line.

senses.head: Dig in — start eating; entrench
senses.body: Two related uses of the same phrasal: an invitation to eat, and a refusal to move. *Dig in your heels* is the stubborn one.
examples: *Dig in* before it gets cold.
The troops *had dug in* along the ridge.
He *dug in* his heels and refused to sign.

senses.head: Press or poke into
senses.body: Of something hard pressing against the body.
examples: The strap *digs* into my shoulder.
She *dug* an elbow into my ribs to shut me up.

senses.head: Take a jab at someone
senses.body: Usually *dig at*; the noun *a dig* is commoner than the verb.
examples: She *digs at* him about the car every chance she gets.
He *has dug at* me about that trip all week.

senses.head: Like, appreciate (slang)
senses.body: Dated American slang out of the 1950s and 1960s, and still perfectly understood. It takes the same strong forms.
examples: I *dig* that record.
He *dug* the whole album the first time he heard it.

ding.gloss: To make a short ringing sound, to put a small dent in something, or to knock someone down a peg.

senses.head: Dent, chip, nick
senses.body: The commonest modern American use, above all of cars. Always regular here: *dinged*.
examples: I *dinged* the car door in the parking garage.
Somebody *has dinged* every corner of that table.

senses.head: Ring, chime
senses.body: The original sense, and the one that once took the strong forms. *Dung* is now archaic and dialectal, and it collides with the plain noun *dung*, meaning manure.
examples: The elevator *dings* at every floor.
Timers *ding* all over the kitchen at six.
The bell *dung* twice and fell silent.
That old clock *has dung* the hour since my grandfather's time.

senses.head: Penalize, mark down, reject
senses.body: Informal American, common in grading, hiring, and admissions.
examples: The graders *ding* you for skipping the citations.
Three schools *dinged* him before he got an offer.

senses.head: Strike a light blow
senses.body: The oldest sense, now archaic on its own but audible behind the dent sense.
examples: Something *had dung* against the hull in the night.
Hail *dinged* the roof of the shed all afternoon.

feed.gloss: To give food to a person or animal, or to supply something steadily.

senses.head: Give food to
senses.body: The core transitive sense.
examples: We *feed* the cats at six.
She *has fed* that stray all winter.
They *had fed* the whole crowd before the speeches started.

senses.head: Eat, graze (of animals)
senses.body: Intransitive, and used of animals rather than people; often *feed on*.
examples: Deer *feed* at dusk.
The larvae *feed* on the underside of the leaf.
Bats *had fed* on the insects around the lamp all night.

senses.head: Supply steadily
senses.body: Of rivers, wires, and data streams — anything that keeps something else running.
examples: The river *feeds* three reservoirs.
Two sensors *feed* data to the controller.
That one server *has fed* the whole network since Tuesday.

senses.head: Feed a meter, feed in
senses.body: Feeding a meter, a printer, or a machine that takes material piece by piece.
examples: He *fed* the parking meter another quarter.
*Feed* the sheet in face down.

senses.head: Feed on, feed off
senses.body: Figurative, of things that grow on what should have stopped them.
examples: The rumor *feeds* on every denial.
The fire *had fed* on dry brush for two days.

senses.head: Support financially
senses.body: A family or a household is the object.
examples: That job *feeds* a family of five.
He *fed* four kids on a mechanic's wages.

senses.head: Be fed up
senses.body: A fixed adjectival participle, always *fed up*, usually *fed up with*. It is never active — you cannot feed someone up in this sense.
examples: I *am fed up* with the noise.
They *had* long *been fed up* with the delays.

senses.head: Pass the ball (sports)
senses.body: Sports commentary, with the receiving player as object.
examples: The point guard *feeds* the post all night.
She *fed* him a perfect ball at the far post.

fight.gloss: To take part in a struggle, physical or otherwise.

senses.head: Fight physically; wage war
senses.body: The literal sense, from a schoolyard scuffle to a war. The past is spelled *fought*, one of the *-ought* family with *bought* and *brought*.
examples: He *fought* in the Pacific.
Two guys *fight* outside that bar every weekend.
The champion *has fought* twice this year.

senses.head: Quarrel, argue
senses.body: No blows involved; usually *fight about* or *fight over* something.
examples: They *fight* about money every January.
We *fought* the whole drive home.

senses.head: Struggle against something
senses.body: The object is a problem rather than a person: a fire, an illness, the traffic.
examples: Crews *fought* the fire for nine days.
She *has fought* the same infection three times.

senses.head: Campaign for or against
senses.body: Political and civic, of long public efforts.
examples: We *had fought* the rezoning for two years before the vote.
The union *has fought* three contract battles this decade.

senses.head: Contest legally
senses.body: American usage lets you *fight a ticket*, *fight a claim*, or *fight a will*.
examples: She *fights* every claim the insurer denies.
He *fought* the ticket and won.

senses.head: Fight back
senses.body: To resist after being attacked; also *fight back tears*, meaning to hold them in.
examples: She *fought back* and the whole thing stopped.
Consumers *have fought back* with a boycott.

senses.head: Fight off
senses.body: To repel something coming at you — attackers, a cold, sleep.
examples: He *fought off* a cold all week.
The company *has fought off* two takeover attempts.

senses.head: Fight one's way
senses.body: Movement achieved by effort, literal or figurative.
examples: We *fought* our way through the crowd.
They *had fought* their way into the semifinals.

find.gloss: To come upon something, to discover it after looking, or to form a judgment about it.

senses.head: Discover after searching
senses.body: The core sense: you were looking, and there it was.
examples: She *found* my keys in the freezer.
We *had found* the leak before the plumber arrived.
Investigators *have found* no evidence of tampering.

senses.head: Come upon by chance
senses.body: No searching implied — the thing simply turned up.
examples: He *finds* good bookstores wherever he goes.
She *found* a twenty in an old coat.

senses.head: Learn, establish as a fact
senses.body: Research and reporting, usually *find that*.
examples: Researchers *found* that the effect disappears after a year.
We *have found* the opposite to be true.

senses.head: Consider, judge to be
senses.body: Takes an object plus a description: *find it odd*, *find him difficult*, *find the class hard*.
examples: I *find* the whole argument unconvincing.
She *found* the class harder than she expected.

senses.head: Return a verdict (law)
senses.body: Legal: a jury *finds* someone guilty, and a court *finds for* one side.
examples: The jury *found* him guilty on two counts.
The court *has found* for the plaintiff.

senses.head: Find oneself in a situation
senses.body: Reflexive, and it says the situation was not planned.
examples: We *found* ourselves in the wrong terminal.
He *has found* himself out of work twice this year.

senses.head: Manage to get (time, money, words)
senses.body: The object is a resource that had to be produced from somewhere.
examples: I cannot *find* the time to read anything.
They *found* the money somewhere.

senses.head: Find out
senses.body: Phrasal, of learning a fact — often one somebody was hiding.
examples: *Find out* what it costs before you sign anything.
She *had found out* about the transfer from a coworker.

senses.head: Reach, arrive at (of a thing)
senses.body: The subject is inanimate and gets where it naturally goes: *water finds its level*, *the shot found the corner*.
examples: Water *finds* its level.
The shot *found* the top corner.

fling.gloss: To throw something hard or carelessly.

senses.head: Throw hard or carelessly
senses.body: The core sense, with force or with indifference behind it. There is no form *flinged*.
examples: Don't *fling* your coat on the floor.
Someone *had flung* a rock through the front window.
The pitcher *flings* it past the batter every time.

senses.head: Move abruptly, throw open
senses.body: Of doors, arms, and heads moved with a single violent motion.
examples: He *flung* the door open and walked out.
She *has flung* her arms around every person in the room.

senses.head: Fling oneself into something
senses.body: Reflexive and figurative: to commit all your energy at once.
examples: She *has flung* herself into the new job.
He *flung* himself into the campaign the day after the funeral.

senses.head: Fling off, fling away
senses.body: To discard abruptly — clothes literally, an advantage figuratively.
examples: He *flings off* his boots the second he gets home.
They *had flung away* a two-goal lead.

floodlight.gloss: To light a large area with broad, powerful lamps.

senses.head: Light a large area
senses.body: Of fields, monuments, and building fronts. Like *light*, it allows a regular *floodlighted*, but *floodlit* is the usual choice.
examples: Crews *floodlight* the field for night games.
They *floodlit* the bridge for the anniversary.
Organizers *have floodlit* the plaza every December since 1998.
The city *floodlights* the courthouse on holidays.

senses.head: Floodlit — bathed in floodlight
senses.body: The participle as an adjective, above all in front of a noun: *a floodlit field*.
examples: The stadium *had* been *floodlit* long before kickoff.
We walked back across a *floodlit* parking lot.

force-feed.gloss: To make a person or animal eat, or to push something on someone who does not want it.

senses.head: Make someone eat
senses.body: The literal sense, from medicine, veterinary care, and prisons. It keeps its hyphen in American writing.
examples: Hospitals *force-feed* patients only as a last resort.
The vet *force-fed* the puppy for three days.
They *had force-fed* the calf until it could nurse on its own.

senses.head: Push information on someone
senses.body: Figurative, usually with a note of resentment about advertising or rote teaching.
examples: Advertisers *have force-fed* us the same jingle all month.
He *force-feeds* his students dates and names.

get.gloss: To obtain or receive something, to become something, or to arrive somewhere — the hardest-working verb in English.

senses.head: Obtain, receive
senses.body: The core sense. American English uses *gotten* for the participle here: *I have gotten three offers*, not *I have got three offers*.
examples: I *get* the mail around noon.
She *got* a raise in March.
He *has gotten* three offers this month.

senses.head: Become something
senses.body: With an adjective: *get tired*, *get dark*, *get better*. The commonest way English says that a state is changing.
examples: This *gets* complicated fast.
It *got* dark before we found the car.
The weather *has gotten* worse since Tuesday.

senses.head: Arrive, reach a place
senses.body: Always with a preposition or *home*: *get to work*, *get there*, *get home*.
examples: What time do you *get* to work?
We *had gotten* halfway to Reno before the tire blew.

senses.head: Fetch, go and bring
senses.body: Transitive, often with two objects: *get me a chair*.
examples: *Get* me a chair, would you?
He *got* his sister from the airport.

senses.head: Understand, get it
senses.body: Informal but universal in speech: *I get it*, *nobody got the joke*.
examples: I *get* it now.
Nobody *got* the joke.
She *has* never *gotten* my sense of humor.

senses.head: Catch an illness
senses.body: The everyday alternative to *contract*.
examples: Everyone in the office *got* the flu.
She *has gotten* strep twice this winter.

senses.head: Cause, persuade, arrange
senses.body: Two patterns: *get someone to do something* (persuade) and *get something done* (arrange for it).
examples: I could not *get* him to sign anything.
We *got* the roof fixed in October.
She *has gotten* the whole team to show up early.

senses.head: Have got — possess
senses.body: Present-tense possession, not a perfect at all: *I've got a car* simply means I have one. This is the one place American English keeps *got* rather than *gotten*.
examples: I *have got* a spare key in the car.
She *has got* two brothers in Denver.

senses.head: Have got to — must
senses.body: Obligation, spoken far more than written, and often reduced to *gotta*. Again *got*, never *gotten*.
examples: You *have got to* see this.
He *has got to* stop doing that.

senses.head: Get + past participle (passive)
senses.body: An informal passive that stresses the event rather than the state: *get hired*, *get married*, *get hurt*.
examples: They *got* married in a courthouse.
Two people *got* hurt in the pileup.
Nobody *has gotten* fired over it yet.

senses.head: Get up
senses.body: To rise from bed or from a seat.
examples: I *get up* at five.
He *had gotten up* before the alarm.

senses.head: Get over
senses.body: To recover from an illness, a shock, or a person.
examples: She never quite *got over* it.
He *has gotten over* the worst of the jet lag.

senses.head: Get by
senses.body: To manage on barely enough.
examples: They *get by* on one income.
We *got by* with a rental for a month.

senses.head: Get along with
senses.body: To have an easy relationship with someone; also *get along* on its own for managing.
examples: The two of them *get along* fine.
He *has* never *gotten along* with his landlord.

grind.gloss: To crush something into powder, or to rub two hard surfaces against each other.

senses.head: Crush into powder
senses.body: Coffee, grain, pepper, meat. The past *ground* is spelled exactly like the noun *ground*, the earth.
examples: I *grind* the beans right before brewing.
She *ground* pepper over the entire plate.
Someone *has ground* coffee into the carpet.
The mill *grinds* corn for the whole county.

senses.head: Rub or scrape harshly
senses.body: Of teeth and of gears — anything that grates under pressure.
examples: He *grinds* his teeth in his sleep.
The gears *ground* every time he shifted.

senses.head: Sharpen or shape on a wheel
senses.body: Trade use: knives, lenses, valves. Do not confuse the past with the separate regular verb *ground, grounded*, meaning to keep a plane or a teenager at home.
examples: That shop *grinds* lenses to order.
They *had ground* the blade down to almost nothing.

senses.head: Grind to a halt
senses.body: A fixed phrase for machinery or an effort stopping slowly and heavily.
examples: Traffic *had ground* to a stop by seven.
The whole project *ground* to a halt in April.

senses.head: Grind down — wear someone out
senses.body: Figurative, of pressure applied long enough to break resistance.
examples: The commute *grinds* people down.
Six months of this *has ground* him down.

senses.head: Grind away, grind out
senses.body: The source of *the daily grind*. Of dull, effortful, repetitive work.
examples: She *grinds* away at the same problem for weeks.
He *has ground out* four hundred pages of the thing.

hang.gloss: To fasten something so that it dangles, or to be suspended.

senses.head: Suspend, put up
senses.body: The transitive core sense, of pictures, coats, and laundry.
examples: We *hang* the wreath the day after Thanksgiving.
He *hung* his jacket on the back of the chair.
They *have hung* new blinds in every room.

senses.head: Be suspended, dangle
senses.body: The intransitive twin of sense 1.
examples: A single bulb *hangs* over the table.
Smoke *has hung* over the valley for a week.
The portrait *had hung* in that hallway since 1962.

senses.head: Execute by hanging
senses.body: This sense alone takes the regular *hanged*. Writing that a painting *was hanged* puts a rope around a canvas.
examples: The state *hanged* him in 1892.
Three men *had* been *hanged* before the pardon arrived.

senses.head: Hang over — loom, threaten
senses.body: Figurative, of debts, deadlines, and suspicion.
examples: The deadline *hangs* over everything this week.
The lawsuit *had hung* over the family for years.

senses.head: Hang out — spend time
senses.body: Informal American, of relaxed, unplanned company.
examples: They *hang out* at the diner after practice.
We *hung out* until the place closed.

senses.head: Hang on — wait; hold tight
senses.body: Two senses of one phrasal: a spoken request to wait, and endurance under pressure.
examples: *Hang on* a second — I have the number here.
She *hung on* through two more rounds of layoffs.

senses.head: Hang up — end a call
senses.body: From the days of a receiver on a hook, and still the ordinary word.
examples: He *hung up* on me.
Nobody *has hung up* a coat in this house in years.

senses.head: Freeze, stop responding
senses.body: Computing, intransitive.
examples: The app *hangs* whenever I open that file.
The terminal *had hung* for ten minutes before I killed it.

heave.gloss: To lift or throw something heavy; of a ship, to move or come to rest.

senses.head: Lift or throw something heavy
senses.body: The everyday sense, and here American English is regular: *heaved, heaved*.
examples: Two men *heave* the crates onto the dock every morning.
He *heaved* the box onto the truck.
They *have heaved* every sandbag on that pile.

senses.head: Rise and fall heavily
senses.body: Of a chest after running, of a deck at sea, of ground buckling in a freeze.
examples: Her shoulders *heaved* with every breath.
The sidewalk *has heaved* where the roots got under it.

senses.head: Heave a sigh
senses.body: A fixed collocation; the object is nearly always *a sigh*.
examples: She *heaves* a sigh every time the printer jams.
He *heaved* a sigh and signed it anyway.

senses.head: Retch, vomit
senses.body: Informal; the noun phrase is *the dry heaves*.
examples: The smell alone makes me *heave*.
He *had heaved* twice before we reached the dock.

senses.head: Move or come to rest (nautical)
senses.body: This is the sense that carries *hove*, and it survives mainly in *hove into view* and *hove to*.
examples: The freighter *hove* into view just after dawn.
The schooner *has hove* to off the point.
By noon the whaler *had hove* alongside.

hold.gloss: To keep something in your hands, or to keep anything at all in a fixed state.

senses.head: Grasp, keep in the hands
senses.body: The literal core sense. There is no form *holded*, and every compound follows suit.
examples: Please *hold* the door.
He *held* the ladder while I climbed.
She *has held* that baby all afternoon.

senses.head: Bear weight, stay fastened
senses.body: Intransitive, of anything under load. Watch the near-twin *hole up*, to hide away, whose past *holed* sounds exactly like *hold*.
examples: That rope *holds* about three hundred pounds.
The shelf *had held* for years before it finally gave.

senses.head: Contain, have room for
senses.body: Capacity, of tanks, rooms, and containers.
examples: The tank *holds* forty gallons.
That room *has held* two hundred people before.

senses.head: Occupy or own
senses.body: Of a job, a title, a degree, a record, or a stake in something.
examples: She *had held* the same job for nineteen years.
He *holds* two patents.
They *have held* a majority stake since 2019.

senses.head: Conduct, stage an event
senses.body: Meetings, elections, hearings, funerals.
examples: The board *has held* four meetings this quarter.
They *held* the election in November.

senses.head: Believe, maintain, rule
senses.body: Formal, usually *hold that*. In legal writing a court *holds* something, and the ruling itself is a *holding*.
examples: The court *held* that the statute did not apply.
Most economists *hold* the opposite view.

senses.head: Remain true or valid
senses.body: Intransitive, of rules, theories, and arguments: *the rule holds*, *that holds true*.
examples: The rule *holds* in every case we tested.
That argument *has held* up remarkably well.

senses.head: Detain, keep in custody
senses.body: Of police, hospitals, and customs.
examples: Police *held* him overnight.
They *have held* the shipment at customs since Monday.

senses.head: Keep back, reserve
senses.body: To withhold or set aside — including the diner sense: *hold the onions*.
examples: *Hold* the onions on mine.
The hostess *held* our table for twenty minutes.

senses.head: Hold a breath, a note
senses.body: To sustain something that naturally wants to stop.
examples: *Hold* your breath for five seconds.
He *held* the note longer than anyone thought he could.

senses.head: Hold on, hold off, hold out
senses.body: Three common phrasals: *hold on* means wait, *hold off* means delay, and *hold out* means last or refuse to give in.
examples: *Hold on* — I have the number right here.
The roof *held out* through the whole storm.
She *has held off* on buying anything until spring.

interbreed.gloss: To breed with a different variety, population, or species.

senses.head: Breed across populations
senses.body: Intransitive, and the ordinary biological sense.
examples: The two populations *interbreed* wherever their ranges overlap.
Wolves and coyotes *interbred* along the Great Lakes.
Biologists say the subspecies *have interbred* for millennia.

senses.head: Cause two lines to breed together
senses.body: Transitive, with a breeder or a research station as the subject.
examples: Breeders *interbreed* the lines to fix the coat color.
The station *has interbred* wheat varieties since the 1930s.

senses.head: Marry within a closed group
senses.body: Of people, and usually with a suggestion of too small a gene pool.
examples: That flock *interbreeds* with the wild birds every spring.
The valley families *had interbred* so long that everyone shared a surname.

lead.gloss: To go in front and show the way, or to be in charge of something.

senses.head: Guide, go in front of
senses.body: The literal sense. The commonest spelling error in American writing is putting *lead* where the past *led* belongs — the metal *lead* is pronounced the same and tempts the fingers.
examples: The ranger *led* us up the switchbacks.
She *leads* the group out at seven sharp.
He *has led* three expeditions to that range.

senses.head: Direct, be in charge of
senses.body: Of teams, departments, and organizations.
examples: She *leads* the Tuesday standup.
He *led* the department for six years.
She *has led* the team since the merger.

senses.head: Lead somewhere (of a road)
senses.body: Intransitive, with an inanimate subject.
examples: This trail should *lead* you straight to the falls.
The clues *had led* us to the wrong house entirely.

senses.head: Lead to — result in
senses.body: Causation, and one of the most common verb phrases in expository writing.
examples: That decision *has led* to a lot of confusion.
One question *led* to another.

senses.head: Be ahead, be in front
senses.body: Sports and polling: *lead by four*, *lead the division*.
examples: They *lead* the division by four games.
She *led* from the first lap to the last.

senses.head: Lead a life
senses.body: A fixed collocation; the object is always a life or an existence.
examples: They *lead* a quiet life out there.
He *has led* an unusually complicated life.

senses.head: Lead someone on
senses.body: To encourage a hope, usually a romantic one, that you do not intend to satisfy.
examples: He *led* her on for months.
Nobody *has led* you on about the timeline.

senses.head: Lead with, lead off
senses.body: Journalism and meetings: to open with a particular item.
examples: Every paper *led with* the same photo.
She *led off* the meeting with the budget.

light.gloss: To set something burning, or to fill a place with light.

senses.head: Set burning, ignite
senses.body: Candles, grills, fires, fuses. Both *lit* and *lighted* are standard American English, but *lit* is the usual past.
examples: We *light* the fireplace on the first cold night.
He *lit* the grill with a long match.
Someone *has lit* every candle on the table.

senses.head: Illuminate, give light to
senses.body: Of lamps and windows. *Lighted* is most at home in front of a noun: *a lighted window*.
examples: That one lamp *lights* the whole room.
The crew *had lit* the runway before the plane turned in.

senses.head: Light up — brighten
senses.body: Of a face with pleasure, or a panel with signals.
examples: Her whole face *lights up* when he calls.
The board *lit up* with warnings.

senses.head: Light a cigarette; light up
senses.body: Informal, and usually with no object at all: *he lit up on the porch*.
examples: He *lit* a cigarette on the porch.
She *has lit up* twice since we sat down.

senses.head: Light on, light upon
senses.body: To come to rest on something, literally or with the eye. Overlaps with the separate verb *alight*.
examples: Her eye *lit on* the one line that mattered.
A moth *had lit* on the screen door.

senses.head: Light out — leave fast
senses.body: Dated American slang, famous from the last line of *Huckleberry Finn*.
examples: They *lit out* for California the next morning.
He *had lit out* before anyone noticed he was gone.

meet.gloss: To come together with someone, or to satisfy a requirement.

senses.head: Encounter, come together with
senses.body: The core sense, whether arranged or by chance.
examples: I *met* her standing in line at the DMV.
We *meet* every other Thursday.
They *have met* twice since the merger.

senses.head: Be introduced to
senses.body: First contact only. Once you have met someone, you *see* them from then on.
examples: *Meet* my brother Danny.
We *met* at a wedding in 2011.

senses.head: Assemble, convene
senses.body: Of a committee, a board, or a class, with the group as subject.
examples: The committee *meets* on the first Monday of the month.
The board *has met* four times this year.

senses.head: Satisfy a requirement
senses.body: The object is a standard, a deadline, a need, or a quota.
examples: This proposal *meets* all three conditions.
He *had met* the deadline by about four minutes.

senses.head: Go to receive an arrival
senses.body: You *meet a flight* or *meet someone at the airport* by being there when they land.
examples: Can you *meet* my flight on Sunday?
She *met* us at baggage claim.

senses.head: Join, come into contact
senses.body: Of roads, rivers, edges, and lines, with inanimate subjects.
examples: The two trails *meet* just above the falls.
The seams *had met* unevenly along the whole hem.

senses.head: Face, encounter (resistance, a fate)
senses.body: Often *meet with*: *met with resistance*, *met his death*.
examples: The plan *met* fierce resistance.
The proposal *has met* with a lot of skepticism.

senses.head: Meet someone's eye; meet halfway
senses.body: Two fixed phrases — refusing eye contact, and compromising.
examples: He would not *meet* my eye all evening.
They *met* us halfway on the price.

mislead.gloss: To give someone a false impression, on purpose or by accident.

senses.head: Deceive deliberately
senses.body: Deception that avoids an outright lie. The past is *misled*, said mis-LED — never spelled *mislead*.
examples: He *misleads* people without ever quite lying.
The label *misled* thousands of buyers.
Nobody *has misled* you about the price.

senses.head: Create a false impression unintentionally
senses.ru: сбивать с толку, вводить в заблуждение (невольно)
senses.body: Of charts, statistics, names, and signs. The adjective *misleading* is commoner than the verb here.
examples: These charts *mislead* more than they explain.
The brochure *had misled* us about the distance to the beach.

senses.head: Lead astray
senses.body: Older and moralizing: to draw someone into bad conduct.
examples: Bad company *had misled* him early.
She swore that nobody *misled* her into signing it.

senses.head: Take a meaning wrongly
senses.body: The core sense, of words, instructions, and intentions.
examples: I *misunderstood* the invitation and showed up a day early.
People regularly *misunderstand* that policy.
She *has misunderstood* my email twice now.

senses.head: Fail to grasp a subject
senses.body: Of a task, a rule, or a body of material rather than a single remark.
examples: Half the class *misunderstood* the assignment.
They *had misunderstood* the terms before they ever signed.

senses.head: Misjudge a person
senses.body: Often passive and sympathetic: *a misunderstood artist*, *a misunderstood kid*.
examples: He *misunderstands* every joke and laughs anyway.
Critics *have misunderstood* her work from the start.
He was a *misunderstood* kid who turned out fine.

outfight.gloss: To defeat someone in combat, or simply to fight better than they do.

senses.head: Beat in a fight
senses.body: The core sense: to win a physical fight, or to prevail over a stronger enemy in war. It follows *fight* exactly, so the past and participle are both *outfought*.
examples: Smaller crews sometimes *outfight* bigger ones.
He *outfought* a taller opponent for twelve rounds.
That regiment *has outfought* every unit it has faced.

senses.head: Outwork an opponent (boxing, MMA)
senses.body: Ring commentary: to land the better and busier work over a bout without necessarily finishing anyone. Extends to any contest won by effort rather than by a decisive blow.
examples: She *outfights* everyone in her weight class without ever knocking anyone out.
The champion *outfought* him on the inside for eight rounds.
Underdogs *had outfought* the favorites for most of the tournament.

outshine.gloss: To be much more impressive than someone or something else, or literally to give off more light.

senses.head: Be far more impressive than
senses.body: The everyday sense, and the one you will meet in reviews and in office talk.
examples: A good opening line can *outshine* a whole chapter.
The understudy *outshone* the lead.
That one dessert *has outshone* everything else on the menu.

senses.head: Give off more light than
senses.body: The literal sense, less common than the figurative one. Only *outshone* in edited prose; *outshined* turns up in speech and in song lyrics.
examples: A full moon *outshines* every star in the sky.
The stadium lights *outshone* the fireworks.
Venus *had outshone* everything else on the horizon by dusk.

overfeed.gloss: To give too much food to a person or animal, or too much of anything to a system that cannot absorb it.

senses.head: Give too much food
senses.body: The literal sense, used of pets, fish, livestock, and guests.
examples: New owners almost always *overfeed* their fish.
We *overfed* the dog over the holidays.
He *has overfed* every guest who ever sat at that table.

senses.head: Oversupply a system
senses.body: Extended to fertilizer, fuel, data, or money — anything supplied faster than it can be used. Before a noun the participle pulls its stress forward: *an overfed market*.
examples: Don't *overfeed* the lawn with nitrogen.
A stuck float *overfed* the carburetor and the engine flooded.
Cheap credit *had overfed* the housing market for years.

overhang.gloss: To stick out over something below, or, figuratively, to loom over it.

senses.head: Project out over
senses.body: Physical: a roof, a branch, or a cliff extending past whatever is under it. It follows *hang* on the *hung* branch only, since there is no execution sense, so ✗ *overhanged* never appears.
examples: Those branches *overhang* the driveway.
A dead limb *overhung* the porch all summer.
The cliff *has overhung* that trail since the last slide.

senses.head: Loom over, weigh on
senses.body: Figurative, usually of debt, suspicion, or a threat that has not yet come to anything. Very common in business writing.
examples: Layoffs *overhang* every conversation in that building.
Debt *has overhung* the company since the buyout.
The lawsuit *had overhung* the merger for two years.

overshoot.gloss: To go past the point you were aiming for, in space or in measure.

senses.head: Go past the target point
senses.body: The literal sense, of drivers, runners, and anything else that travels too far.
examples: Pilots *overshoot* that runway in a crosswind.
We *overshot* the exit by four miles.
She *has overshot* the driveway twice this week.

senses.head: Exceed a limit or estimate
senses.body: Of budgets, deadlines, inflation, and growth — anything that runs past a planned figure. Standard in business and economics writing.
examples: Big projects always *overshoot* their budgets.
Costs *overshot* the estimate by a third.
Inflation *had overshot* the target for six straight quarters.

senses.head: Land long, aviation
senses.ru: проскочить полосу, уйти на второй круг
senses.body: Technical: to touch down too far along the runway, or to fail to land within it at all. The noun and adjective take front stress — *an overshot landing*, *an overshot jaw*.
examples: If you *overshoot*, go around and try again.
The 737 *overshot* the runway in the rain.
Two aircraft *had overshot* before the tower closed the field.

plead.gloss: To answer a criminal charge in court, or to beg someone earnestly.

senses.head: Enter a plea in court
senses.body: Fixed with *guilty*, *not guilty*, or *no contest*, and with no preposition: you *plead guilty*, never ✗ *plead to be guilty*. Both *pled* and *pleaded* are standard American pasts here.
examples: Defendants *plead* not guilty at arraignment.
He *pled* guilty to a lesser charge.
She *has pled* not guilty to all four counts.

senses.head: Beg, appeal earnestly
senses.body: Takes *with* before the person and *for* before the thing: *plead with your boss for more time*.
examples: Don't *plead* with him; he decided a week ago.
She *pled* with the landlord twice this month.
They *had pled* for more time before the judge cut them off.

senses.head: Argue a case as an attorney
senses.body: Formal legal use, and the source of the noun *pleadings*.
examples: She *pleads* every case the same way.
The firm *pled* the matter in federal court.
Counsel *has pled* this issue three times already.

senses.head: Offer as an excuse or defense
senses.body: Fixed objects: *plead ignorance*, *plead poverty*, *plead insanity*, *plead the Fifth*. What is pleaded is the reason you give, not something you necessarily believe.
examples: You cannot just *plead* ignorance and walk away.
He *pled* the Fifth rather than answer.
She *had pled* exhaustion and gone home early.

reshoot.gloss: To film or photograph something over again.

senses.head: Film or photograph again
senses.body: Used of movie scenes and of still photography alike, and it follows *shoot* in every form. The noun *a reshoot* takes front stress: /ˈriˌʃut/.
examples: We *reshoot* anything the client flags.
He *reshoots* every portrait he isn't sure about.
The studio *reshot* the ending twice.
They *have reshot* half the movie.
The crew *had reshot* the scene before lunch.

rewind.gloss: To wind something back toward the beginning, literally or figuratively.

senses.head: Wind tape or film back
senses.body: The original sense, from cassettes and reels; it survives on every video player and podcast app.
examples: *Rewind* it about ten seconds.
He *rewound* the tape and played it again.
I *have rewound* this song four times.

senses.head: Go back over something
senses.body: Figurative, borrowed from the tape sense: to replay a moment in your head, or to restart a conversation. Often an interjection — *rewind, say that again*.
examples: Let's *rewind* to the part where you agreed to pay.
She *rewound* the whole argument on the drive home.
He *has rewound* that conversation a hundred times.

senses.head: Rewire a motor or coil
senses.body: Technical, in electrical and machine-shop work: to replace the winding on a motor, a transformer, or a generator.
examples: A good shop can *rewind* that motor for less than a new one costs.
They *rewound* the armature by hand.
The generator *had* been *rewound* twice before it failed for good.

shine.gloss: To give off or reflect light, or to be conspicuously good at something.

senses.head: Give off light
senses.body: The core intransitive sense, and the one that takes *shone*. Americans say /ʃoʊn/, rhyming with *bone*; the British say /ʃɒn/, rhyming with *gone*.
examples: The porch light *shines* all night.
The sun *shone* through the whole ceremony.
That lamp *has shone* since Tuesday without a break.

senses.head: Gleam, look glossy
senses.body: Of a surface that reflects rather than emits — hair, wet pavement, polished wood.
examples: Her hair *shines* in that light.
The wet street *shone* under the headlights.
The old table *has shone* like new since we oiled it.

senses.head: Excel, stand out
senses.body: Figurative: to be visibly better than everyone around you, especially in a moment that puts it on display.
examples: New quarterbacks rarely *shine* in their first start.
She *shone* in the second act.
He *has shone* in every crisis this company has had.

senses.head: Aim a light at something
senses.body: Transitive, and here the past is the regular *shined*: *she shined the flashlight at us*. ✗ *She shone the flashlight* is not standard American English.
examples: *Shine* the light over here.
He *shined* his phone into the crawlspace.
The deputy *has shined* a spotlight on every car that passes.

senses.head: Polish
senses.body: Always the regular *shined* — *shined shoes*, never ✗ *shone shoes*.
examples: He *shines* his own shoes every Sunday.
She *shined* the silver before the guests came.
Somebody *has shined* every trophy in that case.

senses.head: shine through
senses.body: Of a quality that shows itself despite everything laid over it.
examples: Her patience *shines* through even on the worst days.
His nerves *shone* through in the first ten minutes.
The original color *has shone* through where the paint wore thin.

shoot.gloss: To fire a weapon, to send something moving fast, or to record images with a camera.

senses.head: Fire a weapon; hit with a bullet
senses.body: The core sense, transitive or intransitive. *Shot* is the only past — ✗ *shooted* never appears — and it doubles as an adjective: *shot nerves*, *the clutch is shot*.
examples: They *shoot* skeet out past the tree line.
Someone *shot* out the streetlight again.
He *has shot* competitively since high school.

senses.head: Film or photograph
senses.body: The standard verb in film and photography: *shoot* a movie, a scene, a wedding, a roll of film.
examples: They *shoot* the commercial in Utah.
She *shoots* film, not digital.
The director *had shot* the whole scene before the rain came.

senses.head: Take a shot at a goal or basket
senses.body: Sports. Also used of the score a golfer posts — *he shot a 68* — and of shooting percentages.
examples: *Shoot* from the corner if he leaves you open.
He *shot* the free throw with two seconds left.
She *has shot* forty percent from three all season.

senses.head: Move fast, dart
senses.body: Intransitive, of anything that moves suddenly and quickly — a car, a person, a pain running up an arm.
examples: Kids *shoot* out of that school at three o'clock.
Pain *shot* up my arm.
A cat *had shot* across the road before I could brake.

senses.head: shoot up — rise sharply
senses.body: Of prices, temperature, or a growing child. A separate slang sense of *shoot up*, meaning to inject a drug, is also common and always clear from context.
examples: Prices *shoot up* every summer.
Rent *shot up* forty percent in two years.
He *has shot up* four inches since Christmas.

senses.head: shoot down
senses.body: Literally of an aircraft, figuratively of a proposal or a suggestion.
examples: Anti-aircraft crews *shoot down* what they can see.
The committee *shot down* the proposal in ten minutes.
She *has shot down* every plan we have brought her.

senses.head: shoot for — aim at
senses.body: Informal, of a target date or a goal: *we're shooting for Friday*.
examples: Let's *shoot for* Friday.
They *shot for* a spring release and missed it.
We *have shot for* that number three quarters in a row.

senses.head: Send quickly
senses.body: Informal but very common in American workplaces, with a double object: *shoot me an email*, *shoot her a text*.
examples: *Shoot* me an email when you land.
I *shot* him a text from the parking lot.
She *has shot* me three links already.

senses.head: Put out shoots, of a plant
senses.body: Intransitive and horticultural — the source of the noun *a shoot*, a new green stem.
examples: Bamboo *shoots* up as soon as the ground warms.
The vines *shot* six feet in a single season.
The seed potatoes *have shot* in the bag.

sit.gloss: To rest on your seat, to be positioned somewhere, or to serve as a member of a body.

senses.head: Be seated; take a seat
senses.body: Intransitive: *sit* never takes an object the way *set* does. ✗ *Set down and relax* is dialect, not standard American English.
examples: We *sit* in the back row.
He *sat* through the whole three-hour meeting.
She *has sat* in that same chair for twenty years.

senses.head: Be situated, be located
senses.body: Of buildings, land, and objects at rest. No movement of any kind is implied.
examples: The house *sits* on two acres.
The bowl *sat* on the counter untouched.
The village *has sat* on that ridge since the 1700s.

senses.head: Stay unused, sit idle
senses.body: Of something left where it is for a long stretch, usually with a note of waste — or, of dough and tea, deliberately left to rest.
examples: Let the dough *sit* for an hour.
That box *sat* in the garage for six years.
The application *has sat* on his desk since March.

senses.head: Serve on a body; be in session
senses.body: Takes *on*: *sit on the board*, *sit on a jury*. Of a court or a legislature it means to be in session.
examples: Three of us *sit* on the hiring committee.
She *sat* on the school board for a decade.
The court *has sat* every Tuesday since October.

senses.head: Pose for a portrait; take an exam
senses.body: *Sit for* a painter or a photographer. The exam use — *sit an exam* — is British; Americans *take* one.
examples: He refuses to *sit* for a portrait.
She *sat* for Sargent twice.
That family *has sat* for the same photographer for years.

senses.head: Look after a child, pet, or house
senses.body: Short for *babysit*, and now extended to pets and houses: *sit for the neighbors*, *house-sit*.
examples: I *sit* for the neighbors on Fridays.
She *sat* with their twins all weekend.
He *has sat* for that family since he was fifteen.

senses.head: sit through
senses.body: To stay to the end of something tedious.
examples: Nobody wants to *sit through* another slideshow.
We *sat through* four hours of testimony.
She *has sat through* that movie six times.

senses.head: sit out
senses.body: To take no part in something, especially a game or a vote, by choice or because of injury.
examples: He will *sit out* the rest of the season.
She *sat out* the last two games with a sprain.
They *have sat out* every vote this year.

senses.head: sit up
senses.body: Two uses: to raise yourself from lying to sitting, and to stay awake late. Also figurative — *that made me sit up and take notice*.
examples: *Sit up* straight.
He *sat up* half the night with a sick dog.
The patient *has sat up* on her own since Tuesday.

slide.gloss: To move smoothly over a surface, or to decline gradually.

senses.head: Move smoothly along a surface
senses.body: Intransitive. The participle is *slid*, identical to the past: ✗ *has slidden* is not English, however much *ridden* and *hidden* seem to invite it.
examples: These drawers *slide* all the way out.
The truck *slid* halfway into the ditch.
The door *has slid* off its track again.

senses.head: Push something smoothly
senses.body: Transitive: to move an object across a surface without lifting it.
examples: *Slide* the box under the bed.
He *slid* the envelope under the door.
She *has slid* the same note across my desk twice.

senses.head: Decline gradually
senses.body: Of prices, ratings, standards, or health — a slow slip rather than a crash.
examples: Ratings *slide* every year after the finale.
The stock *slid* eleven percent in June.
His grades *have slid* since he took the second job.

senses.head: Slide into a base
senses.body: Baseball: to drop and skid feet-first or headfirst into a base to get under the tag.
examples: You *slide* headfirst only if you like broken fingers.
He *slid* into second ahead of the throw.
She *has slid* into home twice this week.

senses.head: let something slide
senses.body: Fixed phrase, two ways: to overlook a fault this once, or to let something deteriorate through neglect. The verb itself stays in the base form here.
examples: I'll *let* it *slide* this time.
They *let* the maintenance *slide* for years.
He *has let* his training *slide* since the injury.

sling.gloss: To throw something casually, or to hang it loosely from a support.

senses.head: Throw, hurl casually
senses.body: *Slung* is the past and the participle; ✗ *slinged* is not English, and neither is ✗ *slang*, which in living English is only the noun for informal vocabulary.
examples: The pitcher *slings* it sidearm.
He *slung* the bag into the trunk.
She *has slung* more insults at him than I can count.

senses.head: Hang loosely, suspend
senses.body: Especially over a shoulder or between two points: *sling a rifle*, *sling a hammock*. The noun *a sling*, for an injured arm, comes from this.
examples: *Sling* the strap over your shoulder.
He *slung* his coat over the chair.
They *had slung* a rope across the creek.

senses.head: sling hash, sling drinks
senses.body: Informal American, almost always in these fixed collocations: to serve food or drinks fast and without ceremony.
examples: Cooks *sling* hash at that diner from five in the morning.
She *slung* drinks at a place on Fourth Street all through college.
He *has slung* coffee at the same shop for six years.

senses.head: sling mud
senses.body: Fixed phrase out of politics: to make ugly personal accusations. The noun is *mudslinging*.
examples: Both campaigns *sling* mud in the last two weeks.
They *slung* mud until neither side looked clean.
The tabloids *have slung* mud at her for a decade.

slink.gloss: To move quietly and furtively, often as if ashamed.

senses.head: Move furtively
senses.body: *Slunk* is the standard past and participle; *slinked* turns up occasionally but sounds off to most American ears.
examples: Cats *slink* along the fence line at dusk.
She *slinks* past the office whenever the boss is in.
The dog *has slunk* under the porch again.

senses.head: slink off, slink away
senses.body: The commonest use of the verb: to leave quietly in embarrassment or defeat.
examples: Don't *slink* away when someone calls you out.
He *slunk* out before anyone could ask a question.
They *had slunk* off toward the parking lot.

senses.head: Move sinuously
senses.body: Of a person moving in a deliberately smooth, hip-swaying way — the sense behind the adjective *slinky*. More at home in fiction than in everyday speech.
examples: She *slinks* across a room like she owns it.
The singer *slunk* to the microphone in a long green dress.
Models *have slunk* down that runway all week.

sneak.gloss: To go, take, or do something quietly so that nobody notices.

senses.head: Go somewhere unnoticed
senses.body: Intransitive, usually with a direction: *sneak in*, *sneak out*, *sneak past*. *Snuck* is now the majority American past; *sneaked* is the older regular form and still what conservative editors prefer.
examples: Kids *sneak* into the theater every weekend.
He *snuck* out the back door.
Somebody *had snuck* three extra chairs into the room.

senses.head: Take or do something secretly
senses.body: Transitive: *sneak a cookie*, *sneak a cigarette*, *sneak candy into the movie*.
examples: Don't *sneak* food into the lab.
She *snuck* a cookie off the tray.
He *has snuck* a nap every afternoon this week.

senses.head: sneak up on
senses.body: Of a person approaching unheard, and figuratively of a date or a season that arrives before you noticed.
examples: Deer will let you *sneak up on* them if the wind is right.
The deadline *snuck up on* me.
Winter *has snuck up on* us again.

senses.head: sneak a look, sneak a peek
senses.body: Fixed object: a quick unauthorized glance. The related noun is *a sneak peek*, an early preview.
examples: *Sneak* a look at the answer key if you must.
She *snuck* a peek at the price tag.
He *has snuck* a look at every present under the tree.

speed.gloss: To move very fast, or to make something happen faster.

senses.head: Move fast
senses.body: Intransitive, and the sense that takes *sped*: *the ambulance sped past*.
examples: Cars *speed* down that street all night.
The cab *sped* through the intersection.
The train *has sped* past three stations without stopping.

senses.head: Drive over the limit
senses.body: The traffic offense, most often in the progressive — *she was speeding* — and the source of *a speeding ticket*.
examples: People *speed* through that school zone every morning.
He *sped* the whole way and still got there late.
She *has* been *speeding* on that road for years.

senses.head: Make something happen sooner
senses.body: Transitive and slightly formal: *speed the process*, *speed recovery*, *speed approval*.
examples: Warm weather *speeds* the whole process.
The new law *sped* approval of a dozen projects.
Antibiotics *have sped* his recovery.

senses.head: speed up
senses.body: The everyday phrasal verb. Here Americans use the regular *speeded up* about as readily as *sped up*, and both are correct.
examples: *Speed up* — the light is about to change.
They *speeded up* production after the holidays.
The line *has sped up* since they added a register.

spin.gloss: To turn quickly around a center, to twist fiber into thread, or to give a story a favorable slant.

senses.head: Turn rapidly around a center
senses.body: Intransitive. *Spun* covers both the past and the participle; the old past *span* is dead in American English.
examples: The wheels *spin* on wet leaves.
The dryer *spun* for another twelve minutes.
That fan *has spun* nonstop since June.

senses.head: Make something turn
senses.body: Transitive: *spin a globe*, *spin the wheel*, *spin a coin* on a table.
examples: *Spin* the wheel and see what you get.
She *spun* the globe and stopped it with one finger.
He *has spun* that record so often it skips.

senses.head: Feel dizzy
senses.body: Of a head, and of a room when you are the dizzy one: *my head is spinning*.
examples: My head *spins* when I stand up too fast.
The room *spun* the moment she stood.
My head *had spun* for an hour before I finally sat down.

senses.head: Twist fiber into thread
senses.body: The oldest sense — wool, flax, cotton — and the source of *spinster*, once simply a woman who spun.
examples: They still *spin* their own yarn on that farm.
She *spun* wool all winter.
The mill *has spun* thread on this river since 1840.

senses.head: Spin a web or a cocoon
senses.body: Of spiders and silkworms: the same word as the thread sense, applied to what an animal produces.
examples: Orb weavers *spin* a new web every night.
A spider *spun* a web across the doorframe.
Something *has spun* a cocoon under the eaves.

senses.head: Present with a favorable slant
senses.body: Public relations and politics — the source of *spin doctor* and *put a spin on it*.
examples: Every campaign will *spin* the numbers its own way.
He *spun* a bad quarter into a story about long-term investment.
The press office *has spun* this so hard that nobody knows what happened.

senses.head: spin out
senses.body: Of a vehicle losing traction and rotating, and of stretching something thin over time — *spin out the discussion*.
examples: Rear-wheel-drive cars *spin out* on ice.
The truck *spun out* on the bridge.
Two drivers *had spun out* before the caution flag came.

spit.gloss: To force saliva or something else out of the mouth.

senses.head: Eject saliva
senses.body: American English accepts two pasts: *spit* itself is commoner in speech, while *spat* is the older form and the one this group is built on. Do not confuse the past with the unrelated noun *a spat*, a petty quarrel.
examples: Please don't *spit* on the floor.
He *spat* on the sidewalk and kept walking.
Somebody *has spat* all over this bus window.

senses.head: Eject something from the mouth
senses.body: Transitive, usually with *out*: seeds, pills, gum, bad coffee.
examples: *Spit* out the gum before you go in.
He *spat* out the seed.
She *had spat* the pill into a napkin.

senses.head: Emit in bursts
senses.body: Of engines, fires, and fryers — anything that throws off small bits with force. Also of weather: *it's spitting outside* is a light, spattering rain.
examples: The engine *spits* smoke when it's cold.
The fire *spat* sparks onto the deck.
That old grill *has spat* grease on the wall for years.

senses.head: Say angrily
senses.body: Of speech delivered with contempt, mostly in narration after a quotation.
examples: He can *spit* out an insult faster than anyone I know.
“Get out,” she *spat*.
The coach *had spat* the words at him in front of the whole bench.

senses.head: spit up
senses.body: Of a baby bringing milk back up, or of a person coughing something up.
examples: Babies *spit up* constantly in the first months.
He *spat up* blood and they called an ambulance.
The baby *has spat up* twice this morning.

spotlight.gloss: To shine a narrow beam on something, or to single it out for attention.

senses.head: Draw attention to
senses.ru: привлекать внимание к, выдвигать на первый план
senses.body: The commoner sense in writing today, and the one where Americans reach for the regular *spotlighted*: *the article spotlighted three schools*.
examples: The show *spotlights* local musicians.
The report *spotlighted* three failing districts.
Every profile of her *has spotlighted* the same two years.

senses.head: Light with a spotlight
senses.body: The literal sense, on a stage or from a vehicle, and the one where *spotlit* is normal: *a spotlit dancer*.
examples: They *spotlight* one soloist at a time.
The lighting crew *spotlit* the podium.
Wardens *have spotlit* deer on that road to catch poachers.
A single lamp *had spotlit* the empty chair all evening.

stand.gloss: To be on your feet, to be positioned or situated somewhere, or to remain in force.

senses.head: Be on your feet; rise
senses.body: The core intransitive sense. Watch the vowel: *stood* has the short /ʊ/ of *good*, not the long /u/ of *food*.
examples: We *stand* for the anthem.
She *stood* in line for two hours.
He *has stood* at that counter every morning for years.

senses.head: Be situated
senses.body: Of buildings, monuments, and trees — where something is, with no suggestion of movement.
examples: The barn *stands* where the original house was.
A church *stood* on that corner until 1961.
The statue *has stood* in the square since the war.

senses.head: Place something upright
senses.body: Transitive, usually with a particle or a phrase: *stand it up*, *stand them against the wall*.
examples: *Stand* the ladder against the gutter.
He *stood* the bike against the fence.
Someone *has stood* all the chairs on the tables.

senses.head: Remain in force, still be true
senses.body: Of records, offers, rulings, and invitations: *the offer stands*.
examples: My offer *stands* until Friday.
The old record *stood* for forty years.
That ruling *has stood* since 1974.

senses.head: Tolerate, bear
senses.body: Almost always negative or in a question: *I can't stand it*, *how do you stand him?*
examples: I can't *stand* the smell of that soap.
She *stood* it for about a week and then quit.
He *has* never *stood* being told what to do.

senses.head: stand trial; stand accused
senses.body: Formal and legal, with no article: *stand trial*, *stand accused of fraud*.
examples: He will *stand* trial in the spring.
She *stood* trial for six weeks.
Three executives *have stood* accused of the same scheme.

senses.head: stand to gain, stand to lose
senses.body: Fixed with an infinitive: to be in a position where something is likely to happen to you.
examples: You *stand* to lose the deposit.
They *stood* to make a fortune if the zoning changed.
Investors *have stood* to gain from every one of these delays.

senses.head: stand for
senses.body: Two uses: what an abbreviation means — *what does the D stand for?* — and, in the negative, what you refuse to put up with: *I won't stand for it*.
examples: What does the second D *stand for*?
The flag *stood for* something different then.
The union *has* never *stood for* that kind of scheduling.

senses.head: stand out
senses.body: To be conspicuous, for good or bad.
examples: Bright colors *stand out* in that room.
One name *stood out* on the list.
Her application *has stood out* from the start.

senses.head: stand by
senses.body: Two uses: to stay loyal to a person or a statement — *I stand by what I said* — and to wait ready to act.
examples: Crews *stand by* whenever there's a storm warning.
He *stood by* her through the whole investigation.
The company *has stood by* its numbers.

senses.head: stand up
senses.ru: встать; выдержать проверку; не прийти на встречу
senses.body: Three uses: to rise; to hold up under scrutiny — *the evidence won't stand up in court*; and, informally, to fail to meet someone as arranged.
examples: Everybody *stand up*.
He *stood* her *up* twice.
That theory *has* never *stood up* to a serious test.

senses.head: stand up for, stand up to
senses.body: *Stand up for* someone means to defend them; *stand up to* someone means to face them down.
examples: Somebody has to *stand up for* the new hires.
She *stood up to* her manager in front of everyone.
He *has stood up for* that kid since day one.

stave.gloss: To fend something off, or, of a hull or a cask, to smash a hole in it.

senses.head: stave off
senses.body: The only sense alive in everyday American English, and always the regular *staved off* — never ✗ *stove off*. Of hunger, bankruptcy, or a collapse: to hold it away for a while.
examples: A snack will *stave off* the worst of it.
We *staved off* bankruptcy for another quarter.
They *have staved off* three takeover attempts.

senses.head: Smash a hole in
senses.body: This is the sense that takes *stove*, and it is almost entirely nautical: *the hull was stove in*. The form looks like the kitchen appliance, which is a different word entirely.
examples: One rock can *stave* a wooden hull.
The ice *stove* in the bow.
A drifting log *has stove* a hole in the dinghy.

stick.gloss: To attach or adhere, to push something pointed into something, or to become fixed in place.

senses.head: Adhere, attach
senses.body: *Stuck* is the only past — ✗ *sticked* does not occur in ordinary American English.
examples: These labels *stick* to anything.
He *stuck* a note on the fridge.
The tape *has stuck* better than I expected.

senses.head: Push a point into
senses.body: Of needles, pins, forks, and knives: *stick a fork in it*, *the nurse stuck me twice*.
examples: *Stick* a pin in the map where you were born.
The nurse *stuck* him three times before she found a vein.
Someone *has stuck* a fork in every one of these potatoes.

senses.head: Put, place casually
senses.body: Informal but extremely common in speech: *stick it in the drawer*, *stick it on my desk*.
examples: *Stick* it in the drawer for now.
She *stuck* the receipt in her pocket.
He *has stuck* his bike in the hallway again.

senses.head: Become jammed; be unable to move
senses.body: Of windows, drawers, and vehicles. The participle doubles as an adjective: *a stuck drawer*, *stuck in traffic*.
examples: The bottom drawer *sticks* in humid weather.
The window *stuck* halfway.
We *had stuck* the car in a snowbank by ten in the morning.

senses.head: be stuck with
senses.body: Idiomatic and usually passive: to be left holding something nobody wanted. *Be stuck on* someone, by contrast, means to be infatuated with them.
examples: Don't *stick* me with the check.
They *stuck* us with the cleanup.
I *have* been *stuck with* his old laptop for two years.

senses.head: Take hold, persist
senses.body: Of a nickname, a habit, or a criminal charge: *the name stuck*, *make the charges stick*.
examples: Nicknames like that *stick* for life.
Somebody called him Tiny in third grade and it *stuck*.
None of the accusations *have stuck*.

senses.head: stick to
senses.body: Of a plan, a story, a diet, or a budget.
examples: *Stick to* the plan.
She *stuck to* the same order every time.
He *has stuck to* that story for thirty years.

senses.head: stick out
senses.body: To protrude, or to be conspicuous. *Stick it out* is a different thing: to endure something to the end.
examples: Don't let the wire *stick out*.
His ears *stuck out* under the helmet.
She *has stuck out* three winters in that apartment.

senses.head: stick around
senses.body: Informal: to stay a while longer.
examples: *Stick around* — there's cake.
He *stuck around* until the last guest left.
Nobody *has stuck around* long enough to learn the system.

senses.head: stick up for
senses.body: Informal, and close to *stand up for*. On its own, *stick up* can mean to rob at gunpoint — the noun is *a stickup*.
examples: You have to *stick up for* yourself here.
She *stuck up for* me in the meeting.
He *has stuck up for* his brother his whole life.
